name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,891

clue.text: Convincing suggestion for businessman?

blocks.note: the business half of the word is a company, and CO is how a company signs itself
the man half is a gent, the everyday clipping of gentleman

explanation.walkthrough: The clue never splits the long word for you, and spotting that one word is really two is the whole solve. Six letters, two pieces, no indicator anywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Convincing → COGENT: an argument called cogent is one that compels agreement, which is what a convincing argument does.

clue.text: Examinee may go out taking papers

indicators.note: A word taking something in is holding it, so the letters named next are lodged inside rather than added on the end.

blocks.note: may and can grant the same permission, one word swapped for the other
to go out with somebody is to date them
your papers are your ID, the documents that say who you are

explanation.walkthrough: The exam-hall surface is a decoy. 'Go out' is dating rather than leaving, and the papers are the ones in a wallet, not the ones on the desk.
explanation.definitionFit: Examinee → CANDIDATE: anyone sitting an exam is entered as a candidate for it, which is the word printed on the paper itself.

clue.text: Flush stuck

blocks.note: a face that flushes goes a colour, and the verb comes first
and red is the colour it goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flush' wants to be the definition — level, or well off — but it is the whole of the wordplay, and it has to be heard as two little words rather than one.
explanation.definitionFit: stuck → GORED: a bull that gores has stuck its horn into somebody, so the past tense of that piercing is what 'stuck' names.

clue.text: Negative jerks disregarding good quality of Forrest Gump?

indicators.note: A jerk is a sudden yank, and letters yanked about land somewhere other than where they started.
To disregard something is to leave it out, so the letter named next never joins the shuffle.

blocks.note: the first word is itself the raw material, and it arrives one letter too long for the light
G is the crossword's letter for good, as on an old school report

explanation.walkthrough: 'Negative jerks' reads as an insult aimed at people, and that is the misdirection: the first word is not describing the jerks, it is the letters themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: quality of Forrest Gump → NAIVETE: the film's hero trusts everyone and suspects nothing, so the word is defined by an example of it.

clue.text: Tail Miss Piggy had is splitting

indicators.note: Something splitting comes apart in the middle, so the three letters beside it open up and let another word sit in the gap.

blocks.note: Miss Piggy is a pig, and the word for a female pig is a sow
the clue's own word, dropped in whole at face value

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends the Muppet owns a tail. 'Tail' is really the verb here — to follow somebody about — and the pig is only there for her three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tail → SHADOW: to tail somebody is to follow them everywhere they go, and the verb borrows the name of the thing that already does.

clue.text: Did weed have an energetic dance?

blocks.note: to hoe a bed is to weed it, and 'did' asks for the past tense
to have something is to own it

explanation.walkthrough: Read as English the clue asks whether a plant went dancing; read as wordplay both halves are plain verbs, laid end to end with nothing joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: an energetic dance → HOEDOWN: a hoedown is a fast American square dance, so the definition names the kind of party rather than the steps.

clue.text: Suburban property beginning to dry up, rent cheap place in NYC?

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only one character of what follows is taken.
A down entry reads bottom to top, so what has just been spelled out is read back the other way.

blocks.note: a semi is a semi-detached house, the standard British suburban home
the opening letter of the word, and nothing more of it
rent is what a rip did: the past of rend, which matches the past of tear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to dry up' begs to be read as one phrase about a drought, and the clue cuts straight through it. A dime is the American ten-cent coin the shop is priced by.
explanation.definitionFit: cheap place in NYC → DIME STORE: the American five-and-dime, the cut-price variety shop an American rather than a Briton would name.

clue.text: Slice iron through rolling green

indicators.note: Something rolling tumbles over and over, so the letters it touches come to rest in a different order.
A thing driven through another ends up inside it, so these two letters land in the middle rather than at either end.

blocks.note: green means raw or unripe, and those three letters are the ones tumbled about
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling green' paints a golf course, which is also where a sliced iron shot goes. The whole surface is golf and not one word of the wordplay is.
explanation.definitionFit: Slice → WAFER: a wafer is a thin slice cut off something, the word used for communion bread and for a sliver of silicon alike.

clue.text: Spooner's providing canal-side labour for ridiculous figure

indicators.note: The Oxford don's name marks his trademark accident: the opening sounds of two words trade places and both come out as other words.

blocks.note: the labour on offer is staffing a lock, the gated chamber that lifts boats from one canal level to the next
trade the sounds at the front of those two words, ST for L, and say what comes out

explanation.walkthrough: The joke only works out loud, so say the canal job first and then trade its opening sounds. What comes back is a person nobody takes seriously.
explanation.definitionFit: ridiculous figure → LAUGHING STOCK: somebody everyone laughs at is held up as an object of ridicule, which is what the phrase names.

clue.text: Extravagant old princess wearing fancy clothes

indicators.note: Clothes wrap the wearer, so used as a verb the word puts one set of letters round another instead of beside it.

blocks.note: somebody in a hat is wearing it, so this is the two letters of that little word
fancy as an adjective: heavily decorated
the princess crosswords mean is Diana, and 'old' says the former holder of the title rather than the present one

explanation.walkthrough: Two garment words doing different jobs: one is a two-letter word meaning 'wearing', the other is the instruction to wrap. Only one of them contributes letters of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Extravagant → INORDINATE: an inordinate amount is one past all proper limits, the same excess that 'extravagant' names of spending.

clue.text: Warmer boob

blocks.note: a tube of fur you push both hands into on a cold day
British slang for a silly blunder, and for making one

explanation.walkthrough: Four letters and two everyday senses with no join between them: one is a piece of old-fashioned outerwear, the other is what a fielder does to an easy catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Warmer → MUFF is the fur tube that keeps the hands warm; boob → MUFF is the verb for fluffing something, as in muffing a catch.

clue.text: Reader loving literature superficially

indicators.note: What is superficial sits on the surface, and a word's surface is the pair of letters you see at each end of it.

blocks.note: kind and loving name the same warmth of character
the outside of the word, its opening and closing letters only

explanation.walkthrough: Amazon's e-reader is the definition, so a brand name is standing in for a common noun — and the ordinary verb, to set alight, has nothing to do with the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Reader → KINDLE: definition by example, since the Kindle is one brand of e-reader among several rather than the word for the class.

clue.text: Specialised dictionary idiot brought over in triumph

indicators.note: Something brought over is turned face about, so the letters beside it are written from the back end forwards.
A piece that goes in something sits inside it, buried in the middle rather than added to either end.

blocks.note: a triumph is a glory, the noun rather than the verb the surface offers
an idiot is an ass, and those three letters arrive back to front

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a bad-tempered scholar. The wordplay is kinder: 'triumph' is a thing you have, not a thing you do, and the insult is only there to be turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Specialised dictionary → GLOSSARY: a glossary lists just the terms of one subject with their meanings, which is a dictionary narrowed to a single field.

clue.text: Italian peers east regularly on walk back from Aldi

indicators.note: Taking letters at regular intervals means every other one, so only half the word beside it reaches the grid.
In an across clue a piece that sits on another is written after it, the way one word leans against the next.
The back of a word is its final letter, so one character is taken off the end of the name that follows.

blocks.note: to march is to walk in step
the first and third letters, picked out at every other step
Aldi is a discount supermarket chain, and only the letter it ends on is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a walk home from the shops, and every word of it is doing a separate job. 'Peers' means noblemen here, not people of your own age.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian peers → MARCHESI: marchesi is the Italian plural of marchese, the rank that matches an English marquess, so both words are noblemen.

clue.text: Caroline squirms letting Mike in, a smutty labourer

indicators.note: Somebody squirming will not hold still, and letters that will not hold still come out in an order of their own.
Letting a person into a room admits them inside it, so the letter named next joins the pile before it is shaken up.

blocks.note: the name's eight letters are the bulk of the fodder
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet that pilots and police spell with

explanation.walkthrough: 'Smutty' is literal here — smut is soot and coal dust — which is the opposite of what the surface wants you to hear. Caroline is fodder rather than a character.
explanation.definitionFit: smutty labourer → COALMINER: a worker who comes up black with dust at the end of a shift is the one who has been digging coal.

clue.text: Strip to plunge into boiling water?

definitions.text: Strip to plunge into boiling water?

blocks.note: the surface asks you to picture somebody undressing for a hot bath; read it as a noun and it is a long flat ribbon instead
which is what a cook does with that ribbon — a few minutes in a rolling pan and supper is ready

explanation.walkthrough: No letters are hidden here: the whole sentence is one description read two ways. The same word also means a head, or the fool attached to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue → NOODLE: a noodle is a strip of pasta dough and cooking one means dropping it into boiling water, so clue and answer describe one thing.

clue.text: Thieving needs clear criminal intelligence

indicators.note: Here the word means lawless rather than a person, and letters with no law over them settle in any order at all.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder; the word contributes nothing but them
nous is common sense or brains, a Greek word English helped itself to

explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal intelligence' is a phrase the surface hands you whole, and the clue cuts it in half: one word is the instruction and the other is a piece of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thieving → LARCENOUS: larceny is the lawyer's word for theft, so its adjective describes exactly the habit that 'thieving' names.

clue.text: Still covered with random lace, bride twirled

indicators.note: What is covered is out of sight, and these letters are out of sight underneath the words that carry them.
A twirl spins a thing right round, so the run of letters reads the opposite way from how the clue prints it.

blocks.note: six letters run without a break from the end of the first word to the start of the last, and they arrive facing the wrong way

explanation.walkthrough: The wedding surface does all the work: 'random' looks like a shuffle instruction and 'lace' like its fodder, when in fact the answer is lying right across them.
explanation.definitionFit: Still → BECALM: to becalm is to make calm, and a ship becalmed sits dead still, so the verb answers 'still' in its calming sense.

clue.text: Earth going round sun which is yellow and hot

indicators.note: Something going round travels about the outside of what it circles, so those letters are written around the ones beside them.

blocks.note: earth in the gardener's sense is mud
the sun is a star, the one nearest us

explanation.walkthrough: The surface draws the solar system and the wordplay draws a flowerbed. 'Yellow and hot' belongs to the condiment shelf rather than to any planet's weather.
explanation.definitionFit: yellow and hot → MUSTARD: English mustard is bright yellow in the pot and fiercely hot on the tongue, so the pair of adjectives names it exactly.

clue.text: BBC boss starts to examine tweets stored by Lineker's devices

definitions.note: 'Devices' is plural and the answer is a mass noun covering all of them at once, the same way 'machinery' answers to 'machines'.

indicators.note: The start of a word is its first letter, and this instruction is plural, so one letter comes off each of the two words that follow.
Whatever stores a thing keeps it inside, so the letters just named are shut up in the middle of the name beside them.

blocks.note: Gary Lineker, the England striker turned Match of the Day presenter, is on first-name terms with British viewers
the BBC's boss is its Director-General, DG for short
one letter from the front of each word

explanation.walkthrough: A BBC boss and Lineker's tweets really did make headlines together, which is why the surface reads like news; the pieces of the clue have nothing to do with each other.
explanation.definitionFit: devices → GADGETRY: gadgetry is the collective word for clever little contrivances, so it stands in where a plural naming several of them would.

clue.text: Upsetting bloody film about India's partition

indicators.note: To upset a thing is to tip it over, and a word tipped over in a down entry is read from the bottom square upwards.
One thing about another is wrapped round it, so the single letter goes inside the pair of words rather than after them.

blocks.note: blood is red, so the adjective hands over the colour
India is I in the NATO alphabet
a vid is a video, the everyday clipping

explanation.walkthrough: India's partition is a real event and the whole surface leans on it. In the wordplay the country is only its signal letter, and a partition is a screen in a room.
explanation.definitionFit: partition → DIVIDER: a partition is the screen or panel put up to split one room into two, which is the job a divider does.

clue.text: Planet invaded by second alien creature with tufty ears

indicators.note: An invader gets inside the place it invades, so what follows is pushed into the middle of the word before it.

blocks.note: the planet named after the Roman god of war
a mo is a moment — 'hang on half a mo' — so it does duty for a second
ET is the crossword's standard alien, borrowed from the film

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is science fiction and every piece of it is ordinary: a planet, a moment and a film alien, with the tufted ears belonging to a monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: creature with tufty ears → MARMOSET: the common marmoset is a small South American monkey with white tufts sprouting from each ear.

clue.text: Interrupt Kazakh journalist, giving answer up front

indicators.note: In a down entry the front is the top square, so the letter named beside these words is lifted out of the name and re-laid at the start.

blocks.note: A is the standard short form of answer, as in a Q and A
the fictional Kazakh reporter of the Sacha Baron Cohen film, left without the A that has moved

explanation.walkthrough: Borat is the Kazakh television reporter Sacha Baron Cohen played, and the clue takes his name apart by moving one letter rather than by shuffling the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Interrupt → ABORT: to abort something is to stop it part-way through, which is what interrupting a launch or a program amounts to.

clue.text: Fire's lovely after a ramble

indicators.note: A ramble is a wander with no route in mind, and letters home from one turn up in no particular order.

blocks.note: six letters taken straight from the clue and rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire's lovely' is a sentence about a hearth, and that is the trick: the first word is the definition, the second is raw material, and neither is about warmth.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire → VOLLEY: a volley is a burst of shots let off at once, so the noun in its gunnery sense names the same thing.

clue.text: See interruptions on YouTube much?

definitions.note: 'Much' is a mass quantifier while the answer is plural in shape; both fill the same slot — 'not much to do', 'loads to do' — so the swap is fair.

blocks.note: lo is the old imperative for look, as in 'lo and behold'
what breaks into a video you are watching for free

explanation.walkthrough: Reading the clue as one exasperated question is the trap. It splits after the first word, and the rest is simply what free video keeps handing you.
explanation.definitionFit: much → LOADS: in casual speech loads means a large amount — 'thanks loads' — so it stands where the quantifier would.

clue.text: Last member of 1950s radio comedy

definitions.note: The second definition works on the four letters run together, not on the two words the grid splits them into — same letters, different spacing.

blocks.note: the verb: to endure, to carry on, the way a supply lasts a week
one of the cast of the anarchic BBC radio show that ran through the fifties — Milligan, Sellers, Secombe and Bentine

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the whole game: two words in the grid, one word on the wireless. The Goon Show's name gave English a word for a thug and a fool alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Last → GO ON: a meeting that goes on lasts; the radio sense needs the same letters closed up into one word, the name of a Goon.

clue.text: Vagrant had race against senior minister

indicators.note: A vagrant has no fixed address, and letters with no fixed address are free to settle anywhere in the light.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, taken from the two words as they stand
the con of 'pros and cons' is the case against

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vagrant had race' sounds like a story about a tramp, and only the first word of it is an instruction. The rest is letters, plus the crossword's usual word for opposition.
explanation.definitionFit: senior minister → ARCHDEACON: an archdeacon ranks above the parish clergy in the Church of England, so 'minister' is meant in its churchy sense.

clue.text: Harangue weary assistant on the phone

indicators.note: Words down a telephone reach you as sound only, so what counts is how they are heard rather than how they are spelt.

blocks.note: a weary helper is a tired aide, and said at speed the two words run into one

explanation.walkthrough: Say the two words quickly and the join disappears. The surface, an exhausted office junior taking a call, exists only to hide where one word stops and the next starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Harangue → TIRADE: a harangue is a long angry speech aimed at somebody, and a tirade is that same outburst under another name.

clue.text: Conservative is revolting in difficult moments

blocks.note: C is the ballot-paper abbreviation for a Conservative candidate
a population that is revolting rises against its rulers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' is the political verb here rather than the adjective the surface offers, and 'Conservative' is a party letter rather than a temperament.
explanation.definitionFit: difficult moments → CRISES: a crisis is the moment when a situation comes to a head, and the plural covers several such turning points.
